etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lot, from Old English hlot (“portion, choice, decision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.

Cognate with North Frisian lod, Saterland Frisian Lot, West Frisian lot, Dutch lot, French lot, German Low German Lott, Middle High German luz. Doublet of lotto. Related also to German Los.

definitions.definition: A large quantity or number; a great deal.

quote.citation: 1877, William Black, Green Pastures and Piccadilly, volume 2, page 4:
quote.text: He wrote to her  […]  he might be detained in London by a lot of business.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter III, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC, page 52:
quote.text: I filled my dreener in no time, and then it come to me that 'twouldn't be a bad idee to get a lot more, take 'em with me to Wellmouth, and peddle 'em out.

definitions.definition: A separate, appropriated portion; a quantized, subdivided set consisting a whole.
One or more items auctioned or sold as a unit, separate from other items.
(informal) A number of people taken collectively.
A distinct portion or plot of land, usually smaller than a field.

quote.citation: 1820, James Kent, edited by William Johnson, Reports of cases adjudged in the Court of Chancery of New-York‎[3], volume 5, published 1822:
quote.text: The defendants leased a house and lot, in the City of New-York

definitions.definition: That which happens without human design or forethought.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “(please specify the book), Canto V”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 1:
quote.text: But save my life, which lot before your foot doth lay.

definitions.definition: Anything (as a die, pebble, ball, or slip of paper) used in determining a question by chance, or without human choice or will.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 16:33:
quote.text: The lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: If we draw lots, he speeds.

definitions.definition: The part, or fate, that falls to one, as it were, by chance, or without one's planning.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book XI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: O visions ill foreseen! Each day's lot's / Enough to bear.

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book III”, in [Alexander Pope], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume I, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: He was but born to try / The lot of man — to suffer and to die.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, chapter II, in The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, book III:
quote.text: […]  as Jones alone was discovered, the poor lad bore not only the whole smart, but the whole blame; both which fell again to his lot on the following occasion.

quote.citation: 1977, C-3PO, Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope:
quote.text: We seem to be made to suffer. It's our lot in life.

quote.citation: 1694 November 22 (Gregorian calendar), John Evelyn, “[Diary entry for November 12 1694]”, in William Bray, editor, Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn, […], 2nd edition, volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […]; and sold by John and Arthur Arch, […], published 1819, →OCLC:
quote.text: In the lottery […]  Sir R. Haddock one of the Commissrs of the Navy had the greatest lot, £3000 ; my coachman £ 40

quote.citation: 1990: Donald Kagan, Pericles of Athens and the Birth of Democracy, chapter 2: “Politician”, page 40 (Guild Publishing; CN 2239)
quote.text: Archons served only for one year and, since 487/6, they were chosen by lot. Generals, on the other hand, were chosen by direct election and could be reelected without limit.

definitions.definition: (definite, the lot) All members of a set; everything.
(historical) An old unit of weight used in many European countries from the Middle Ages, often defined as 1/30 or 1/32 of a (local) pound.
(transitive, dated) To allot; to sort; to apportion.
(US, informal, dated) To count or reckon (on or upon).

pronunciation: Received Pronunciation, General Australian, New Zealand, Canada
Boston, Western Pennsylvania, Standard Southern British
